passages.happening:
God sends Moses to Pharaoh again: “Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. But if you refuse to let them go, I will plague your whole country with frogs” (verses 1-2).

The frogs will come “into your palace and up to your bedroom and onto your bed, into the houses of your officials and your people, and into your ovens and kneading bowls” (verse 3).

“So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt. But the magicians did the same thing by their magic arts” (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
English Bibles number this chapter differently from the Hebrew. The Hebrew begins chapter 8 four verses later, so English 8:1-4 is Hebrew 7:26-29. If you compare a Jewish translation, that is why the numbers do not match.

Frogs multiplied in Egypt as the Nile's floodwaters went down. They were part of nature, and also part of religion. The goddess Heqet, linked with birth and fertility, was pictured as a frog or with a frog's head. A land overrun by frogs is fertility turned into a curse.

Listen to where the frogs go: the palace, the bedroom, the bed, the ovens, the bowls where bread was kneaded. No place is private. The plague reaches the king himself.

Once again the magicians copy the sign. And once again, think about what that means. They bring up more frogs. They cannot take any away.
passages.later:
Israel's songs remember it: “Their land teemed with frogs, even in their royal chambers” (Psalm 105:30). “He sent swarms of flies that devoured them, and frogs that devastated them” (Psalm 78:45).

Revelation uses frogs as a picture of evil: John sees “three unclean spirits that looked like frogs” (Revelation 16:13).
passages.asks: The magicians could add frogs but not remove them. Ask whether you have ever tried to answer a problem by adding more of the same. And ask where you need, instead, the God who can take the trouble away.

passages.happening:
“Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, ‘Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from me and my people. Then I will let your people go, that they may sacrifice to the LORD’” (verse 8).

Moses says, “You may have the honor over me”, and asks Pharaoh to name the time when he should pray for the frogs to be taken away (verse 9). “‘Tomorrow,’ Pharaoh answered. ‘May it be as you say,’ Moses replied, ‘so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God’” (verse 10).

Moses cries out to the LORD, and the frogs die. “They were piled into countless heaps, and there was a terrible stench in the land” (verse 14).

“When Pharaoh saw that there was relief, however, he hardened his heart and would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
For the first time Pharaoh asks for prayer, and for the first time he promises to let Israel go. Something has moved in him.

‘You may have the honor over me’ is a polite courtly phrase. Moses lets Pharaoh choose the time. That rules out chance. If the frogs leave at exactly the hour Pharaoh names, he will know ‘that there is no one like the LORD our God’.

And Pharaoh's answer is ‘Tomorrow’. Not now. One more night with the frogs. There is a touch of dark humor in the telling.

Then the relief comes, and it brings its own misery. Heaps of dead frogs and a stench over the whole land.

And then the turn: ‘When Pharaoh saw that there was relief ... he hardened his heart’. This is the first time the text says Pharaoh hardened his own heart. The verb is the one for making heavy. The moment the pressure lifts, the promise is gone.
passages.later:
Israel's later history remembered Pharaoh's hardness as a warning. When the Philistines suffered under God's hand, their priests said, “Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs?” (1 Samuel 6:6).

Moses prays for the king who oppresses his people. Jesus later taught, “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Exodus does not predict that teaching, but it shows it.
passages.asks: Pharaoh promised to obey while he was suffering, and forgot as soon as relief came. Ask whether you have made promises to God in a hard time that you let go when things got easier. And ask what it would mean to keep faith with God after the relief comes.

passages.happening:
God tells Aaron to strike the dust with his staff, “that it may turn into swarms of gnats throughout the land of Egypt” (verse 16). He does, and “gnats came upon man and beast” (verse 17).

“The magicians tried to produce gnats using their magic arts, but they could not” (verse 18).

“‘This is the finger of God,’ the magicians said to Pharaoh. But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
This is the third plague of the first group, and like the third in each group it comes with no warning.

What were these creatures? The Hebrew word may mean lice, gnats or mosquitoes. Translations differ. The BSB says gnats.

Now comes a turning point. The magicians, who copied the first two signs, try and fail. And they say it out loud: ‘This is the finger of God’. The experts of Egypt admit that a power beyond theirs is at work. After this they drop out of the contest until the boils, when they cannot even stand before Moses.

But Pharaoh does not listen, even to his own experts. His heart was hard. Here again the text does not say who hardened it.
passages.later:
The ‘finger of God’ appears again at Sinai. The tablets of the law were “inscribed by the finger of God” (Exodus 31:18).

Jesus picks up the magicians' words. Accused of casting out demons by the power of Satan, he answers, “But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke 11:20). Matthew has “by the Spirit of God” (Matthew 12:28). Jesus is saying that the power that humbled Pharaoh is at work in him, setting captives free.
passages.asks: Even Pharaoh's experts said, ‘This is the finger of God’, and he still would not listen. Ask whether you have seen God at work and still refused to change. And ask whose honest voice you may need to listen to, even if it is not the voice you want to hear.

passages.t: Swarms of flies, and Goshen spared
passages.happening:
Moses meets Pharaoh at the water early in the morning (verse 20). If Pharaoh will not let the people go, “I will send swarms of flies upon you and your officials and your people and your houses” (verse 21).

“But on that day I will give special treatment to the land of Goshen, where My people live; no swarms of flies will be found there. In this way you will know that I, the LORD, am in the land. I will make a distinction between My people and your people” (verses 22-23).

“And the LORD did so. Thick swarms of flies poured into Pharaoh’s palace and into the houses of his officials” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
This begins the second group of three, and as before it starts with a morning meeting at the water.

The Hebrew word for this plague means a swarm or a mixture. The ancient Greek translation took it as a biting dog-fly. Some Jewish interpreters thought it meant a mixture of wild animals. The BSB, like most English Bibles, says flies.

Something new happens here. God makes ‘a distinction’. Goshen is spared. Goshen was where Jacob's family settled in the eastern Nile Delta. Many scholars place it around a valley running east from the Delta toward Sinai, good land for flocks. From now on, the plagues fall on one people and not on the other, living side by side.

This matters to the story's claim. The plagues are not just disasters that happen to hit Egypt. They are signs. They pick out whom they strike. ‘In this way you will know that I, the LORD, am in the land.’ The LORD is not a god of one place far away. He is here, in Egypt.
passages.later:
The distinction between God's people and Egypt reaches its height on the night of the Passover: “I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13).

Peter calls the church “a people for God’s own possession” (1 Peter 2:9), using words first spoken of Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:5).
passages.asks: God said, ‘I, the LORD, am in the land’, in the middle of Egypt. Ask whether you believe God is present where you are, even in a place that feels far from him. And ask what it would look like for your life to show that God makes a difference.

passages.happening:
“Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, ‘Go, sacrifice to your God within this land’” (verse 25).

Moses says no: “the sacrifices we offer to the LORD our God would be detestable to the Egyptians. If we offer sacrifices that are detestable before the Egyptians, will they not stone us?” (verse 26). They must go three days into the wilderness (verse 27).

Pharaoh answers, “I will let you go and sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness, but you must not go very far. Now pray for me” (verse 28).

Moses prays, and the flies are removed, “not one fly remained” (verse 31). “But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time as well, and he would not let the people go” (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
Watch how Pharaoh bargains. First he asked for prayer and promised release (verse 8). Now he says: sacrifice, but inside Egypt (verse 25). Then: go, but not very far (verse 28). Every offer keeps the slaves within reach. He never quite says no, and he never truly says yes. This is how a hard heart bargains.

Moses explains why worship could not happen in Egypt. Israel's sacrifices would be ‘detestable to the Egyptians’. Genesis already says that Egyptians would not eat with Hebrews (Genesis 43:32), and that shepherds were detestable to them (Genesis 46:34). Some interpreters add that certain animals, such as the Apis bull and rams linked with the god Amun, were sacred in Egypt, so that offering such animals in the open could lead to violence. That is exactly what Moses fears: ‘will they not stone us?’

Moses warns Pharaoh not to act ‘deceitfully again’ (verse 29). He prays anyway, and God answers completely: not one fly is left. And Pharaoh hardens his heart again. The text says plainly that he did it himself.
passages.later:
Joseph's brothers had met the same custom: “the Egyptians would not eat with the Hebrews, since that was detestable to them” (Genesis 43:32).

Hebrews warns believers against the same hardness: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15).
passages.hard:
Can the plagues be explained as natural events, and if so, are they still miracles?

Since the nineteenth century many readers have noticed that the first plagues look like a chain. The best-known version was worked out by the scholar Greta Hort in the late 1950s. On this view an unusually high Nile flood, carrying red earth and tiny organisms, turned the river red and killed the fish. Frogs fled the fouled water and died. Insects bred in the rotting heaps. Disease spread by insects struck the livestock and caused sores. The later hail, locusts and darkness, perhaps a great sandstorm, belong to the Egyptian seasons that follow.

Others reject such accounts as missing what the text claims: a series of direct acts of God with no natural cause.

Many take a middle way. The Bible itself names natural means for some of God's acts, such as the east wind that brings the locusts (10:13) and drives back the sea (14:21). So natural causes and God's action are not opposites in Scripture. What makes the plagues signs, on this view, is not that nature is absent. It is their force, their timing and their precision. Each is announced ahead, begins and ends at Moses' word (Pharaoh even picks the hour in verse 10), and from the fourth plague on, each spares Goshen while striking the rest of Egypt.

These notes do not choose between these readings. On every one of them the text's claim is the same: the God of Israel rules the powers Egypt feared and worshiped.
passages.asks: Pharaoh kept offering half-measures, to keep control. Ask whether you have been offering God a half-obedience: yes, but not too far; yes, but not here. And ask what it would mean to let go of the control you are holding on to.
